blocks.text: Quick verdict

ProxyEmpire is the better buy for anyone who wants raw residential or mobile proxies: it costs a fraction of Nimble's per-GB rate, supports SOCKS5, publishes its pool size and never expires your prepaid traffic. Nimble is only the better option if you specifically want managed extraction, such as its SERP and e-commerce APIs or the Nimble Browser, and you are happy to pay for results instead of bandwidth. For most scraping teams with their own code, ProxyEmpire delivers far more for the money.

ProxyEmpire and Nimble both sell residential proxies, but they are aimed at opposite ends of the market. ProxyEmpire is a mid-market proxy network competing on price, rollover bandwidth and free ISP targeting. Nimble (Nimbleway) is an AI-driven web-data platform whose proxies sit underneath scraping APIs, a managed browser and data-services contracts. If you are comparing them, the real question is whether you want to run your own scraper on cheap IPs or pay more for a service that returns structured data.

blocks.text: ProxyEmpire in 2026: what you get

ProxyEmpire sells residential, mobile, static residential and datacenter proxies from one dashboard and competes on flexibility. Traffic you prepay never expires, ISP-level targeting is free, and the $1.97 trial lets you test both residential and mobile networks before committing. Its 30M+ advertised pool is smaller on paper than the enterprise providers, but independent testing has rated its real reachable pool well relative to its claims.

Strengths: Prepaid traffic rolls over indefinitely; ISP/ASN targeting included at no extra cost; Cheap $1.97 trial covering residential and mobile; Unlimited residential option priced per day. Weak spots: Smaller advertised pool than the big three; Exact GB thresholds for each tier only shown at checkout; Weaker results on Google in some independent tests.
Nimble in 2026: what you get

Nimble (Nimbleway) is an AI-first web-data platform. It offers residential proxies with fast response times and unlimited concurrency, but most of its product investment goes into the Nimble Browser, SERP and e-commerce APIs, and data-services plans that start in the thousands of dollars per month. It does not disclose its residential pool size, and its per-GB rates are among the highest here, so it competes on finished results rather than cheap traffic.

Strengths: Strong managed APIs and an AI-driven browser; Unlimited concurrency on proxies; Credits shared across all Nimble products; Free 5,000-page API trial. Weak spots: No published pool size; HTTP/HTTPS only, no SOCKS5 on proxies; High per-GB price for raw residential traffic.
Pricing: ProxyEmpire vs Nimble

ProxyEmpire's rotating residential pricing currently starts at $3.50/GB (shown as 50% off a $7 list price) and steps down through several tiers to $1.50/GB at 1 TB, with custom pricing from about $0.75/GB above 5 TB. Rotating mobile starts at $4.50/GB, rotating datacenter at about $0.65/GB, and a flat-rate unlimited residential plan is sold by the day.

Nimble's plan cards list residential proxy traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go, falling through credit packages ($150 and $600 entry packages) toward $5.30/GB; its current developer documentation lists $5.30/GB for residential traffic without a commitment. Annual billing saves 15%. Its scraping APIs bill $0.90 to $1.45 per 1,000 URLs depending on rendering.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $35 with ProxyEmpire and $53 with Nimble: a 34% saving in ProxyEmpire's favour. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because ProxyEmpire does not publish an exact price for that volume; Nimble comes to about $530. The sticker price is only half of it. ProxyEmpire's unused traffic carries forward, while Nimble's does not (credits usable across nimble products), so if your usage swings from month to month ProxyEmpire can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Nimble does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. ProxyEmpire lists '30M+' and Nimble lists 'Not published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, ProxyEmpire lists 170+ countries and Nimble lists Worldwide. On targeting, ProxyEmpire offers country, region, city and ISP/ASN (included by default), while Nimble offers country, state and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. ProxyEmpire supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Nimble offers HTTP, HTTPS. If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in ProxyEmpire's favour. On sessions, ProxyEmpire offers rotating or sticky sessions up to 24 hours, and Nimble offers auto-rotation by default; sticky sessions available. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With ProxyEmpire: stable connections and traffic that never expires. With Nimble: its managed APIs remove much of the anti-bot work. Run the same small test on both before committing.

SERP and rank tracking: Nimble wins. The deciding factor for Nimble: its SERP API and search agents return structured results. The limitation on the ProxyEmpire side: Google was its weakest target in independent tests.

Social media and multi-account management: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: residential and mobile IPs with 24-hour sticky sessions. How Nimble compares: no SOCKS5 and a high per-GB cost make it a poor fit for account work.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. ProxyEmpire: free city and ISP targeting. Nimble: dedicated e-commerce data APIs. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Ad verification and geo-testing: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: ISP-level targeting at no extra cost. How Nimble compares: good geo targeting but no published pool data.
Tight budgets: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: rollover means nothing you pay for is wasted. How Nimble compares: per-GB rates are among the highest here.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile. Nimble: Free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs. Verification and payment rules differ too. ProxyEmpire: Standard verification. Nimble: Sales-led onboarding for data-services plans. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test ProxyEmpire and Nimble before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle ProxyEmpire vs Nimble faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile; Nimble: free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs).

2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day. 3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, ProxyEmpire comes out ahead in 3, Nimble in 1, and 2 are ties. That makes ProxyEmpire the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: ProxyEmpire is strongest for teams that hate losing unused bandwidth, while Nimble is strongest for teams that want structured data rather than raw IPs. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
